*After the MD*

# FMGE and NExT: the exam, the internship, the registration

A Philippine MD does not let you practise in India on its own. You pass the screening exam, do a one-year internship in India, then register with a state medical council. NExT is notified but deferred. Plan for the sequence, not the rumours.

*Reviewed 27 November 2026. Rules and dates here come from NMC and NBEMS documents, linked at the foot of the page. Check the current bulletin before you act. [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) — reuse with attribution to drdreams.in.*

**Quick summary.**

A Philippine MD does not give an Indian graduate the right to practise in India on its own. You clear FMGE, or NExT when it is notified, complete a one-year compulsory rotating medical internship in India, and then get permanent registration from a state medical council. FMGE is conducted by NBEMS; the 2002 screening test regulations require 50 per cent in each paper, and the current attempt rules sit in the NBEMS bulletin. NExT was notified in the Gazette on 27 June 2023 and deferred by NMC on 13 July 2023 till further directions; its regulations describe a computer-based Step 1 of six papers and a clinical Step 2 of seven subjects, with both steps to be cleared within ten years of joining the MBBS course. NMC says it does not endorse any list of foreign medical colleges, and it listed 51,121 CRMI slots for foreign graduates for 2026–27 as on 31 October 2026. As of 2026, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Haryana do not require the Indian internship if the student completed it in the Philippines; this is subject to change, so confirm it in writing with the state medical council.

## FMGE, in short

Conducted by
:   NBEMS

Frequency
:   Twice a year

Format
:   Computer based, three papers of multiple choice questions

Pass mark
:   50 per cent in each paper

After passing
:   Provisional registration, then a 12 month internship in India

Then
:   Permanent registration with a state medical council

**The part people skip.**

Passing FMGE does not make you a registered doctor in India. NMC's March 2026 notice says a state medical council cannot grant permanent registration until it has verified the exam, the clerkship and the one-year internship.

The order is fixed: exam, provisional registration, CRMI, permanent registration. Budget two to three years after graduation, and more if you need a second attempt.

*The exams*

## FMGE and NExT, stated plainly

FMGE is a screening test for Indian citizens and Overseas Citizens of India who hold a primary medical qualification from outside India. It has been required for registration since 15 March 2002. It covers the Indian MBBS syllabus, which overlaps with what you learn in the Philippines but is not the same course. The differences are what catch people: Indian public health and forensic medicine, and the Indian legal and ethical framing of clinical questions.

The screening test regulations set three papers of multiple choice questions in pre-clinical, para-clinical and clinical subjects, in English, with 50 per cent required in each paper. Dates, the current syllabus and the attempt rules are announced by NBEMS, so read the bulletin for your year instead of an old regulation or a coaching post.

NExT is the National Exit Test. NMC notified the regulations on 27 June 2023 and then deferred the exam on 13 July 2023, till further directions from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The regulations describe two steps: a computer-based Step 1 with six papers in medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynaecology, paediatrics, ENT and ophthalmology, and a clinical and viva Step 2 covering those six plus orthopaedics and physical medicine. Both steps have to be cleared within ten years of joining the MBBS course. NExT is meant to serve both as the licence exam and as the entrance for postgraduate seats. When it is in force, the corresponding older exam is phased out, but NMC can keep the old exam running for earlier batches.

**What this means for your batch.** You will sit whichever exam is in force when you graduate. As of this review, NExT stands deferred. That is not a reason to wait. The syllabus behind both exams is the same Indian MBBS syllabus, so start with the work, not the name.

*The rules*

## What NMC actually says

**NMC does not endorse a foreign college list.** It says so on its own [study-abroad page](https://www.nmc.org.in/page/information-desk-for-students-to-study-abroad). The old MCI list is not a seal of approval. For screening test eligibility, the regulations accept a qualification named in the World Directory of Medical Schools or confirmed by the Indian embassy in that country as a recognised qualification. Check both. Get the fee structure, course content, duration and internship terms directly from the college in writing.

**The NEET result is the eligibility certificate.** For admissions from May 2018, the NEET-UG result stands in for the eligibility certificate. NMC says that result stays valid for three years from declaration and covers a pre-medical or language course followed by the MBBS. Keep the scorecard with the rest of the file.

**The date you joined decides the rulebook.** The Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate Regulations took effect on 18 November 2021. Join after that date and you are governed by the CRMI Regulations 2021, which require one year of internship in India. Join on or before that date and you can be assessed under the older screening test rules, provided the online classes were compensated physically and you did a year of internship at the foreign college.

**The paperwork is checked, not assumed.** NMC's 6 March 2026 notice says a compensation certificate must name the subjects and duration of theory, clinical work and clerkship. The transcript must be apostilled and authenticated by the Indian embassy. The state council verifies physical presence from visa stamps and passport entry and exit records.

**A state council, not NMC, registers you.** The March 2026 notice puts the job with the state medical council in consultation with the state directorate of medical education. The order is fixed: pass the exam, get provisional registration for CRMI, finish the year, then collect permanent registration. No council may grant permanent registration before those checks are complete. A few states currently waive the Indian year; see the internship section below.

**The seats exist.** NMC published [51,121 CRMI slots](https://nmc.org.in/crmi-slots-for-fmgs) for foreign medical graduates for 2026–27 as on 31 October 2026. Its 2023 notice says the number of seats is 7.5 per cent of permitted MBBS seats in older colleges and 100 per cent in new colleges without their own interns. Allotment is handled by the state council and the DME together, and NMC says foreign graduates draw the same stipend as Indian interns at that institution. The delay comes from applications and verification, not from a shortage of notified seats.

**Two deadlines to note.** The December 2023 NMC notice says the internship must be completed within ten years of joining the foreign medical institution. NExT's regulations set the same ten-year window from MBBS admission for clearing both steps. NMC also published a draft FMGL amendment on 17 November 2026 proposing to change clause 4(b) of the 2021 regulations. A draft is not the final rule. Check the final gazette before you rely on it.

*The plan*

## Five years, in slices

1. ### Year one: one subject, one hour

   Pick anatomy and physiology. Watch Indian lectures for the topics your college is covering that week. You are not preparing for an exam yet. You are learning the Indian vocabulary for the same facts.
2. ### Year two: add pathology and pharmacology

   Two to three hours a week, no more. Start a question bank and do ten questions a week. Keep a notebook of the ones you get wrong. That notebook becomes your revision list later.
3. ### Year three: clinical subjects begin

   Now the ward and the exam point the same way. When you see a case, read the Indian guideline for it that evening. This is the year the two curricula stop feeling like separate courses.
4. ### Year four: full question banks and past papers

   Timed weekly tests. Ten years of past papers at least. Join or form a group of three or four and teach each other, because teaching is the only way to find out what you do not actually know.
5. ### Internship year: revision and mock exams

   Six to eight hours a day in the months before the exam, with mock tests on the same schedule as the real one. This is when the notebook from year two earns its keep.

**Resources, without the brand war.** Marrow, PrepLadder and DAMS are the Indian platforms students most often use, alongside past papers from NBEMS. DrDreams is not affiliated with any of them and is not saying one is better. Pick one and finish it. Collecting three subscriptions is not preparation.

*What works*

## Habits that clear it

One resource, finished. Students who fail usually have four subscriptions and no completed course. Questions from the start, because reading without testing yourself feels productive and is not. A study group of three or four; ten becomes a social club. Timed mocks on the real schedule, because the exam is a stamina test as much as a knowledge test. Clinical work taken seriously, because the viva and the case discussion are where weak training shows.

*What fails*

## Habits that sink people

"I will start after graduation." By then the basic sciences you need most are two years cold. Only watching videos: video feels like studying, recall is studying. Ignoring community medicine, which is a large, boring, high-scoring block. Studying alone for two years; isolation is a bigger risk than a noisy group. Planning around NExT rumours instead of studying the syllabus.

*Coaching*

## Which colleges include it

Five of the six colleges covered here run FMGE coaching on campus: Gullas, Perpetual, DMSF, Brokenshire and Jose Maria, with the last two being smaller programmes. Southwestern does not. Check the current arrangement with the college before you assume either way.

On-campus coaching is worth more than it sounds, because it solves the discipline problem rather than the content problem. If your college does not have it, budget for an online course and treat the subscription as a fixed monthly cost, the same way you treat rent.

[Compare the six on coaching](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md)

## The order of events

Graduation is not the finish line. The route from a Philippine MD to an Indian white coat has four gates, and they happen in a fixed order:

1. Graduate with the MD from a college that meets the foreign medical graduate requirements.
2. Pass FMGE, or NExT when it is in force.
3. Complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship in India.
4. Get permanent registration from a state medical council.

You cannot swap the order. You cannot do the Indian internship before the exam. You cannot register before the internship. And none of it fixes a college that did not meet the requirements when you joined. If you have not checked that yet, read [is the degree valid in India](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#validity) first.

## The twelve month Indian internship

After passing the exam, you get provisional registration and complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship, usually called CRMI, at an approved institution in India. It rotates through medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynaecology, paediatrics, community medicine and the allied departments.

Indian hospitals use this year to see whether your clinical training was hands-on. Students who spent five years watching from a corridor feel the difference in the first month. Students who clerked, presented and assisted in the Philippines settle in faster. NMC says foreign graduates at this stage receive the same stipend as Indian interns at that institution.

Apply early. Allotment runs through the state medical council and the state directorate of medical education, states have different processes, and the gap between passing the exam and starting the internship can be months. Ask both offices for the current process in writing.

**State exception, as of 2026.** Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Haryana do not currently require CRMI from a graduate who has completed the internship in the Philippines. Two conditions matter here. The internship in the Philippines must actually be done, with a certificate and logbook to show for it. And the position is as of 2026 only; state councils can change it. Get the current rule in writing from the state medical council before you plan around it, and keep the Philippine internship documents with your registration file.

## Register with a state medical council

With the exam passed and the internship complete, you apply for permanent registration with the state medical council where you intend to practise. Registration is the legal step that makes you a doctor in India. It is separate from the degree, the WDOMS listing and the exam.

Keep the paper trail: degree, transcript, apostilled documents, the compensation certificate if you studied online, internship certificate, migration certificate, exam pass certificate, and the WDOMS and embassy records from your enrolment year. Registration offices can ask for documents years later, and a college that has changed administration may be slow to reissue them.

## PG in India

If you want an MD or MS in India, the route is NEET-PG. Foreign graduates usually need to clear FMGE or NExT and complete the Indian internship before they are eligible, but the eligibility rules are set in the current NEET-PG information bulletin. Read it for your year, not a summary from a coaching centre. NExT's regulations say the exam will also be used for postgraduate entrance when it is in force.

PG preparation is a different exam from FMGE. FMGE tests the undergraduate syllabus; NEET-PG tests applied clinical decisions in more detail. Most students take a year or two of internship and preparation before sitting it. Starting early is an advantage, but burning out in first year is not.

## Jobs after registration

Once registered, the ordinary options are:

- **Hospital medical officer.** Private and charitable hospitals hire registered doctors for ward duty, emergency and outpatient work.
- **Primary care and clinics.** General practice, family clinics and community health centres.
- **Government health schemes.** State health departments and national programmes hire medical officers on contract and permanent roles.
- **Corporate and insurance medicine.** Medical officers for companies, hospitals and health insurers, including claims and hospital review work.
- **Clinical research and medical writing.** A less clinical path that values a medical degree and clear writing.
- **Hospital administration and public health.** Usually after an additional degree or diploma.

None of these are guaranteed by the degree. They are the normal destinations for a registered Indian doctor, and the competition is the same as for any other graduate.

## Options abroad

A Philippine MD is also a starting point for licensing routes elsewhere. Each has its own exam, fees and eligibility rules, and each should be checked at the official source for your year.

- **United States:** USMLE steps and ECFMG certification. The college's WDOMS listing matters.
- **United Kingdom:** PLAB and GMC registration.
- **Australia:** AMC examinations and registration.
- **Canada:** MCC examinations and provincial licensing.
- **Philippines:** the Physician Licensure Examination and registration with the Professional Regulation Commission. [The PLE, in detail](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines/index.md).

These routes are expensive and slow, and they are not a fallback for a failed FMGE. Decide early if one of them is your plan, because the exam preparation starts years before graduation.

## If you do not clear the exam

It happens, and it is not the end of your medical career. The first step is to check the current attempt rules in the NBEMS bulletin, because they decide what you can do next. The second is to diagnose why you failed: not enough clinical exposure, weak pre-clinical foundations, exam technique, or simply starting too late.

Then build a plan with a date. A repeat attempt with a fixed schedule, question bank targets and weekly tests is very different from "I will study harder". If you are working while preparing, protect two uninterrupted hours a day and one long test every week. The doctors who clear on a second attempt change the method, not just the hours.

## A realistic timeline

From graduation to registration, with the waiting time included.

| Stage | Typical time | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Graduate and collect documents | 1 to 3 months | Degree, transcript, clerkship and compensation certificates, migration certificate |
| Prepare and sit FMGE or NExT | 6 to 12 months | Indian syllabus, question banks, weekly tests |
| Get provisional registration and apply for CRMI | 1 to 3 months | State council and institution applications |
| Complete CRMI | 12 months | Rotations, logbook, certificate |
| Get permanent registration | 1 to 3 months | State medical council application |

The whole sequence usually takes two to three years after graduation. Plan for it financially before you leave for the Philippines, not after you return.

*Check the source*

*Questions*

## After graduation, in plain answers

**Is FMGE difficult for Philippines graduates?**

It is difficult for everyone. Most candidates do not clear it on the first attempt. The ones who do usually started in the early years. The exam tests the Indian MBBS syllabus, which overlaps with yours but is not the same course.

**Has NExT replaced FMGE yet?**

No. NMC notified the National Exit Test regulations on 27 June 2023 and deferred the exam on 13 July 2023, till further directions from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Do not plan around a date from a coaching site. Check the current NMC notice before you act.

**What happens after I clear FMGE?**

You get provisional registration to do a one-year compulsory rotating medical internship in India. After you complete it, the state medical council grants permanent registration. NMC's March 2026 notice sets that order and says the council must verify the exam, the clerkship and the internship first.

**Can I work in India right after the MD?**

No. You need to pass FMGE or NExT, complete the twelve month Indian internship, and register with a state medical council. Only then can you practise.

**Can I do PG in India after a Philippine MD?**

Yes, through NEET-PG, usually after clearing FMGE or NExT and completing the Indian internship. Check the current NEET-PG information bulletin for eligibility. NExT's regulations say the exam will also be used for postgraduate entrance when it is in force.

**What if I fail FMGE?**

Check the attempt rules in the current NBEMS bulletin, diagnose why you failed, and build a fixed study plan with a date. Many doctors clear on a later attempt. It costs time and money, not your career.

**Do I have to do the internship in India?**

Yes, for Indian registration in most states. The Philippine internship is part of the MD. The Indian CRMI is a separate twelve month requirement after the exam. As of 2026, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Haryana do not require it if the internship was completed in the Philippines. State positions can change, so get confirmation in writing from your state medical council. Where CRMI applies, NMC's December 2023 notice says it must be completed within ten years of joining the foreign medical institution.

**Can I practise in the Philippines instead?**

Yes, since November 2026. The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission now permits Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools to sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise in the country, which the Embassy of India in Manila confirmed. The PLE licences you in the Philippines only. To practise in India you still sit FMGE or NExT and finish the twelve month internship. [The PLE, in detail](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines/index.md).

*For current students*

# Study resources and how to prepare

A study framework for the five and a half years, plus the terms your college, the NMC and your seniors use. Nothing here is a paid course, and nothing is downloadable yet.

*Reviewed 25 November 2026.*

**This section is being built.**

Subject notes, question banks and practical guides will be added here as they are prepared. Nothing is downloadable yet, and no file on this page is a promise of what is coming. The study framework below is ready to use now.

## On this page

1. [The subject map, year by year](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#map)
2. [How the Philippine curriculum is taught](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#taught)
3. [A weekly study system](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#system)
4. [Using Indian resources alongside](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#indian)
5. [FMGE from first year](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#fmge)
6. [Learning on the ward](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#clinical)
7. [Notes and downloads](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#coming)
8. [Glossary of terms](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#glossary)

## The subject map, year by year

Philippine medical schools follow the American shape: pre-clinical sciences, then para-clinical sciences, then clinical rotations, then internship. The names and the order vary a little between colleges, so treat this as the common pattern and confirm the exact sequence with your own curriculum.

The usual subject sequence in a Philippine MD programme.

| Stage | Subjects | What it feels like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First year | Anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, histology, embryology, medical ethics | Volume. You are memorising a new language and a new body at the same time. |
| Second year | Pathology, pharmacology, microbiology, parasitology, forensic medicine, community medicine, physical diagnosis | The mechanisms click, and the clinical vocabulary starts to make sense. |
| Third year | Medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and gynaecology, radiology, psychiatry, dermatology | Wards, clerkships, patient histories, and the first time you present a case. |
| Fourth year | Clinical rotations, specialities, review, internship preparation | You are in the hospital most days. The exam is closer than it feels. |
| Internship | Rotating departments under supervision | Long shifts, real responsibility, and the transition from student to doctor. |

Your college may call the years Level 1 to Level 4, or use a different split. The fee sheets from Gullas, DMSF, Jose Maria and Brokenshire use "Level 1" and semesters. That is an administrative label, not a different course.

## How the Philippine curriculum is taught

Most colleges use lectures, laboratory sessions and small-group discussions in the pre-clinical years, then ward-based teaching in the clinical years. The lecture is the skeleton. The learning happens in the laboratory, the group work and the past papers.

Two local habits are worth adopting. The first is the "trans" or transcription: students rewrite or summarise lecture material into a shared document. It is efficient, and it is also how a batch builds a common set of notes. The second is recitation: faculty ask questions in class, and you are expected to answer. If you are shy, practice answering aloud before you go.

Attendance rules are stricter than many Indian students expect. A missed laboratory or ward session can cost you the subject, not just the notes. Read the college's attendance policy in the first week, not the week before the exam.

## A weekly study system

The students who do well do not study more hours than everyone else. They study with a rhythm. A simple system that survives a five and a half year course:

1. **Preview before the lecture.** Ten minutes with the headings is enough. You will recognise the words instead of hearing them for the first time.
2. **Rewrite the lecture the same day.** A one-page summary in your own words, not a copy of the slide.
3. **Do questions twice a week.** Start with the topics you covered that week, not the whole syllabus.
4. **Keep one review day.** Sunday morning for the week's summaries, and nothing new.
5. **Teach one topic to a friend.** If you cannot explain it without the notes, you do not know it yet.

A repeatable week, not a timetable you abandon in week two.

| Day | Focus | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday to Friday | Preview, lecture, same-day summary | 2 to 3 hours outside class |
| Tuesday and Thursday | Questions on the week's topics | 45 minutes each |
| Saturday | Practical or ward notes, weak topic | 2 hours |
| Sunday | Weekly review, one past paper | 2 to 3 hours |

Adjust the hours to your college. The point is the repetition, not the number.

## Using Indian resources alongside

Indian textbooks are cheaper, more exam-oriented and closer to the FMGE syllabus. Philippine textbooks are closer to your lectures and your local exams. Use both, but do not try to read both cover to cover.

A practical split: use the Philippine material to pass the college exam, and one Indian review book per subject to keep the FMGE vocabulary alive. For anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, pathology, pharmacology and microbiology, an Indian review book plus your lecture notes is usually enough for the college exam. For community medicine and forensic medicine, the Indian syllabus differs more, so follow your college first and bridge later.

Do not buy a new set of books every year. A good review book, a question bank and your own notes beat a shelf of unopened titles.

## FMGE from first year

The FMGE clock starts in first year, whether you like it or not. The exam tests the Indian undergraduate syllabus, and the subjects you learn in first year are the ones you will have forgotten by the time you graduate.

You do not need to study for FMGE every day in first year. You need to keep the Indian thread alive: one review book per subject, a question bank you add to slowly, and a note of the topics your Philippine course does not cover. By the clinical years, that thread is the difference between a six month revision and a two year panic.

The [FMGE and NExT page](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next/index.md) has the full year-by-year plan.

## Learning on the ward

Clinical years reward a different skill from pre-clinical years. You are not memorising a list. You are learning to ask a question, examine a patient, and present a plan. Three habits that help:

- **Carry a small notebook.** Write the case in your own words after you see it. The act of writing is the learning.
- **Present every case you can.** Even to a fellow student. The first ten presentations are terrible. The eleventh is better.
- **Ask one question per ward round.** Not to show off. To make yourself follow the reasoning.

Foreign students are allowed hands-on work in Philippine hospitals, which is one of the reasons to choose the country. Use that access. Watching is not the same as doing, and the difference shows up in the exam and in your first Indian internship.

## Notes and downloads

This page will hold subject-wise notes, question banks, practical and OSCE guides, and study planners. They will be added as they are ready, and each file will say which subject and year it covers. Nothing is uploaded yet, so there is no download link to click and no email form to fill.

If you have notes from your own college that you are willing to share, the [contact page](https://drdreams.in/about/index.md#contact) explains how to send them. They will be checked before they are published, and you will be credited if you want to be.

*Questions*

## Study questions students ask

**Are Philippine medical books different from Indian books?**

The content is the same medicine, but the emphasis and the exam style differ. Use Philippine material for your college exams and one Indian review book per subject to keep the FMGE syllabus familiar.

**When should I start FMGE preparation?**

First year, slowly. One review book per subject and a question bank you add to over time. The students who start in the final year are the ones who run out of time.

**Are the notes on this page free?**

The study material will be free when it is added. Nothing is downloadable yet, and there is no paid course behind this page.

**What is a "trans" in a Philippine medical school?**

A transcription, usually a student-made summary of a lecture shared with the batch. It is useful, but it is not a substitute for the lecture or the textbook.

**How many hours a day should I study?**

Two to three focused hours outside class is a realistic baseline. More matters less than consistency and active recall. A weekly review day is worth more than a late-night cram.

[### Glossary

The terms your college, the NMC and your seniors use.](https://drdreams.in/study-resources/index.md#glossary)

**How to use this page.**

If a college email, an NMC notice or a senior uses a term you do not know, find it here. The links go to the page that explains the thing, not just the word.

Terms are grouped by their first letter. Each entry is one or two sentences, because the point is to let you read the next page without stopping.

## A

APMC
:   Association of Philippine Medical Colleges. The association of medical schools in the Philippines, not an Indian regulator.

Apostille
:   A stamp that authenticates a public document for use in another country. India is part of the Hague Apostille Convention, so many Indian documents are apostilled by the Ministry of External Affairs rather than legalised by an embassy.

## B

BSBio
:   Bachelor of Science in Biology, the pre-medical year some Philippine universities offer. It is not a medical degree and it does not replace NEET.

## C

CHED
:   Commission on Higher Education, the Philippine government body that oversees higher education, including medical schools.

Clerkship
:   The clinical years of the MD, when students rotate through hospital departments and clerk patients under supervision.

CRMI
:   Compulsory Rotating Medical Internship. The twelve month internship in India that foreign graduates complete after passing FMGE or NExT.

## E

ECFMG
:   Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates. The body that certifies international medical graduates for US residency applications.

## F

FMGE
:   Foreign Medical Graduate Examination. The screening exam Indian foreign graduates sit before registration. Conducted by NBEMS.

FMGL 2021
:   The Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate Regulations, 2021. The NMC rules that apply to students who enrolled on or after 18 November 2021.

## I

Internship
:   The supervised final year of the MD in the Philippines, done in a hospital. Separate from the Indian CRMI.

## L

Level
:   The administrative name some Philippine colleges use for a year of the MD, as in Level 1 or Level 2. It is not a different qualification.

## M

MD
:   Doctor of Medicine. In the Philippines, the primary medical degree, roughly equivalent to MBBS for Indian registration when the college is NMC-listed.

MEA
:   Ministry of External Affairs, India. It authenticates or apostilles documents for use abroad.

## N

NBEMS
:   National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences. The body that conducts FMGE, NEET-PG and other postgraduate medical exams in India.

NEET
:   National Eligibility cum Entrance Test. The Indian entrance exam for medical courses. NMC requires it for Indian students who intend to practise in India.

NEET-PG
:   The Indian entrance exam for MD, MS and diploma postgraduate seats.

NExT
:   National Exit Test. The exam being introduced to replace FMGE and unify the final-year and licensing examinations. Check the current status for your batch.

NMC
:   National Medical Commission. India's medical regulator since 2020, replacing the Medical Council of India.

## O

OSCE
:   Objective Structured Clinical Examination. A practical exam with stations that test history taking, examination and communication.

## P

PGI
:   Postgraduate Institute. A term used loosely for postgraduate medical institutes. Not a qualification by itself.

PRC
:   Professional Regulation Commission, the Philippine body that licenses professionals, including physicians.

## R

Recitation
:   The classroom habit of being called on to answer questions aloud. Common in Philippine medical schools.

RLE
:   Related Learning Experience. The supervised clinical practice hours built into Philippine health courses. The term is more common in nursing than in medicine.

Rotation
:   A block of clinical training in one department, such as medicine, surgery or paediatrics.

## S

Semester
:   Half of an academic year. Philippine colleges often quote fees per semester rather than per year.

## T

Trans
:   A student-made transcription or summary of a lecture, shared within a batch.

## U

USMLE
:   United States Medical Licensing Examination. The exam series for US medical licensure, usually taken alongside ECFMG certification.

## W

WDOMS
:   World Directory of Medical Schools. A directory of medical schools run by WFME and FAIMER. NMC uses it for verification.

## 9

9F visa
:   The Philippine student visa category. Many students enter on a temporary visa and convert to 9F after enrolment, so confirm the current process with the college and embassy.

### Short answers, if you are in a hurry

- It takes five and a half years and costs Rs 28 to 35 lakh.
- The college must be on the NMC list, checked by you, on the day you enrol.
- NEET is required to practise in India. The BS Biology year does not replace it.
- The teaching is in English. Life in Cebu and Davao is cheaper than Manila.
- After the MD you come home, clear FMGE or NExT, and do a year of internship.

## What is MBBS in the Philippines called?

The degree is a Doctor of Medicine, or MD. It is the Philippine equivalent of the Indian MBBS and it is what Indian students mean when they say MBBS in the Philippines. Filipino colleges also run a separate four-year pre-medical bachelor's degree, usually BS Biology, which their own students take before the MD.

The MD runs five and a half years including the internship, is taught in English, and is open to foreign students who have finished class 12 with Physics, Chemistry and Biology. On paper it is a postgraduate degree. In practice, for an Indian student arriving after class 12, it is a single continuous programme from first year to internship. [The full guide to the degree](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines/index.md).

## How long does MBBS take in the Philippines?

Five and a half years: four years of classroom and clinical study, then a twelve-month internship in a hospital attached to the same university. Students who take the BS Biology year first add another year.

NMC's Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate Regulations require the foreign course to run at least 54 months of academic study, excluding internship, and the internship to be completed at the same institution. A 5.5-year MD satisfies both if you finish on time. The whole thing has to be completed within ten years of joining, including any repeated year, so a lost year is survivable but not free. [What the 2026 notice changed](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md).

## What does MBBS in the Philippines cost?

Between Rs 28 lakh and Rs 35 lakh for the whole programme, for most students at the six colleges on this site. College fees are Rs 20 lakh to Rs 24 lakh of that, and hostel, food, flights and renewals make up the rest.

Those lines are hostel, food, flights twice a year, visa renewals, health insurance, FMGE coaching where it is not included, and a buffer for the emergency nobody plans for. The cheapest college and the most expensive one differ by about eight lakh over five and a half years. That is a real gap, but it is smaller than most quotes suggest, because flights and living costs are the same wherever you go. [Line by line, with a worksheet](https://drdreams.in/fees-and-cost/index.md).

## Is MBBS from the Philippines valid in India?

Yes, if the college is on India's NMC list when you enrol and when you graduate, and if you clear FMGE or NExT and then complete a twelve-month internship in India. Skip any of those and the degree will not get you registered to practise.

The NMC list is the whole test. A college that is not on it produces a degree India will not recognise, whatever a brochure says. Check the list yourself on the NMC site and cross-check the college on WDOMS, then keep the screenshot with the date on it. [The six colleges, with their NMC status](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md).

## What are the latest NMC rules for Philippines graduates?

The rules that matter are the Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate Regulations 2021 and the NMC public notice of 5 March 2026. Together they require a course of at least 54 months, a twelve-month internship at the same foreign university, WDOMS listing, and a twelve-month compulsory rotating internship in India after you clear FMGE or NExT.

The body was called the Medical Council of India, or MCI, until 2020, so older posts still say MCI rules for the Philippines. The rules now come from the NMC. The body was called the Medical Council of India, or MCI, until 2020, so older posts still say MCI rules for the Philippines; the rules now come from the NMC. If you joined before 18 November 2021, the older Screening Test Regulations apply to you. If you joined on or after that date, the 2021 regulations apply in full. The 2026 notice tightened verification rather than banning anyone, and it is the reason you should keep every admit card, fee receipt and attendance record from your college. [The notice, explained with the official PDF](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md).

## Can I study MBBS in the Philippines without NEET?

You can start, but you cannot finish and practise in India without it. Some colleges admit students to the BS Biology year without NEET, and the student clears NEET before moving into the MD. NMC requires NEET for Indian students who want to practise in India, with no exceptions.

The BS Biology route is useful for a student who missed the exam or scored too low for a seat, and it costs an extra year and about three to four lakh rupees. It buys time to prepare. It does not replace the exam. [How the BS Biology route works](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#without-neet).

## Which colleges in the Philippines are taking admissions for 2027?

All six colleges covered here are accepting applications for the 2027 intake. Philippine medical colleges run one main intake a year, with classes beginning in August and September, and applications stay open through the spring until seats fill.

The practical deadline is not the application form. It is the visa appointment and the document authentication, both of which take weeks. A student who applies in June for an August start is usually too late. February to May is the working window. [Compare the six, including fees and hospital size](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md).

## What documents do I need to apply?

Class 10 and 12 marksheets, NEET scorecard, passport with eighteen months of validity, birth certificate, medical certificate, police clearance, passport photographs, proof of funds, and the college's application form with a short personal statement.

The birth certificate and marksheets usually need notarisation, state attestation and a Ministry of External Affairs apostille before the embassy will accept them, which takes two to four weeks. [The full checklist with formats](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#documents).

## Is it safe to study MBBS in the Philippines?

For a student living in a hostel near campus, in Cebu, Manila or Davao, yes. The bigger risks are traffic, petty theft and bad decisions at two in the morning, not violence against foreign students. Thousands of Indian students have lived there for years without incident.

Practical rules that actually keep you safe: live within walking distance of campus or on a well-lit main road, use Grab instead of unlicensed taxis at night, do not carry a laptop in a backpack on a jeepney, keep your documents in a hostel safe, and tell someone where you are going. The cities are not dangerous in the way the news makes them sound. They are not so safe that you can be careless, either. [What daily life is actually like](https://drdreams.in/student-life/index.md).

## Is the course taught in English?

Yes. Lectures, textbooks, examinations and hospital records are in English, and English is one of the two official languages of the Philippines. Filipino and Bisaya are spoken in corridors and canteens.

The first month is hard anyway. Professors speak English with a Filipino accent, patients mix in Bisaya, and the speed takes getting used to. Most students understand two thirds of the first lectures and everything by the end of the first semester. Nobody fails for the accent. [More on the language problem](https://drdreams.in/student-life/index.md).

## Do I need to learn Filipino or Bisaya?

No. You can complete the degree in English. Learning a hundred words of Bisaya or Tagalog will change your hospital experience, though, and patients will treat you differently for trying.

Clinical years are where it matters. A patient who understands your question answers it. A patient who does not gives you a nod and a guess. Ordering food, asking directions and haggling in the market are the other places a little language goes a long way.

## Is FMGE compulsory after I come back?

Yes, if you want to practise in India. Foreign medical graduates sit FMGE or, once it is fully in place, NExT, then complete a twelve-month internship in India, then register with a state medical council.

The pass rate is low, in the range of one in five to one in four in most sessions. Most of that is timing: students start preparing in final year. The ones who clear it begin in first year, with Indian textbooks alongside the Philippine ones. [A study plan by year](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next/index.md).

## Can I work in the Philippines after graduating?

Yes, since November 2026. The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission now permits Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools to sit the Physician Licensure Examination (PLE) and register to practise in the country. The Embassy of India in Manila confirmed the change. Before this, Philippine law required India to give Filipino doctors the same right, and it did not, so the route was closed.

The PLE gives you a licence to practise in the Philippines. It does not register you in India: to work here you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month internship, whichever route you take. If you want to stay, prepare for the PLE the way you prepare for FMGE, from first year. Confirm the current eligibility with the Professional Regulation Commission and your college before you rely on it. [How the Philippine licence works](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines/index.md).

## What is the difference between MD in the Philippines and MBBS in India?

On paper, the Philippine MD is a postgraduate degree and the Indian MBBS is an undergraduate one. In practice both are five and a half years with an internship, both are taught in English, and both lead to a licence only after a qualifying exam and internship in the country where you want to work.

The real differences are clinical and cultural. Philippine hospitals let students do hands-on work early, which Indian colleges often do not. The trade is that you do your internship in the Philippines and then repeat a year of internship in India after FMGE, so the whole path is longer than the Indian one by about a year. [The complete comparison](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines/index.md).

## How much does living in the Philippines cost per month?

Less than most Indian cities for rent, more for groceries. A shared or hostel room, food, transport, phone data and the occasional night out come to a modest monthly figure, and the hostel is where students either save or overspend.

In Cebu and Davao a basic hostel is cheap and a comfortable one is not. Manila costs more for everything except food, and the traffic costs you time you will not get back. Cooking for yourself is the single biggest saving, and the reason a college with an Indian mess works out cheaper than its tuition suggests. [The full cost breakdown](https://drdreams.in/fees-and-cost/index.md).

## When should I start applying for the 2027 intake?

Start in December or January for an August 2027 start. By February you should know your shortlist, by March you should have the college's conditional acceptance, and by May your visa file should be at the embassy.

The order that works: check NMC and WDOMS first, email the colleges, get the document list in writing, start authentication while you wait, sit NEET if you have not, then apply for the visa as soon as the acceptance letter arrives. Every year a batch of students misses the intake because they began in June. [The step-by-step timeline](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md).

## Can my parents visit me during the course?

Yes. They can apply for a visitor visa, and most colleges will issue an invitation letter if the admissions office is asked in advance. Flights are cheapest booked two to three months out, and December and January are the expensive weeks.

A visit in the first semester is worth more than it sounds. Parents who have seen the hostel, met the warden and eaten in the mess stop worrying, and students who are not managing a worried phone call every night do better in first year.

## What happens if I fail a subject or lose a year?

You repeat the subject, usually in a summer term or with the next batch, and you pay for the repeat. The degree does not disappear. What you cannot do is stretch the whole programme past ten years from the date you joined, because NMC will not recognise a course that took longer.

One repeated subject is common and recoverable. Three lost years is a different problem. If you are failing, the fix is almost always the same: fewer hours in the hostel, more hours in the library, and an honest conversation with the faculty before the exam rather than after it.

## Can Indian graduates take the Philippine PLE now?

Yes, since November 2026. The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission permits Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools to sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise in the Philippines. The Embassy of India, Manila confirmed the change.

The PLE licences you in the Philippines, not in India. To practise in India you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month Indian internship. The licence matters if you want the option to stay and work in the Philippines, or if you want your file to satisfy every NMC condition while you are there. [How the licence is obtained](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines/index.md).

## What is the BSBio route, and does it replace NEET?

The BSBio is a pre-medical bachelor's degree, usually BS Biology, that a student straight out of class 12 takes before the MD. It does not replace NEET. NMC still requires NEET for an Indian student who wants to register and practise in India.

The Philippine MD is a postgraduate course: it needs a bachelor's degree and the NMAT. The BSBio year gives you both the degree and time to prepare for NEET. If you take it, get the transfer conditions in writing, including which credits count and how many years it adds. [The route in full](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#without-neet).

## Where to go next

*If your question is not on this page, send it. Questions that keep coming up get added here with the answer.*

[Read the full guide](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines/index.md)
[Ask a question](https://drdreams.in/about/index.md#contact)

*Living there*

# Student life in the Philippines: first month, food, rent and safety

The first month in the Philippines goes to adapting and learning everyday chores, not anatomy: a SIM card, a room and a canteen you can eat from. This page gives shared-room rent, hostel and Indian food costs, safety figures, and the practical differences between Cebu, Manila and Davao.

*Reviewed 27 November 2026. Ground detail from Cebu, Manila and Davao, with weather data from PAGASA and prices from Numbeo. Figures change, so check the sources before you budget. [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) — reuse with attribution to drdreams.in.*

**Quick summary.**

The first month in the Philippines goes to adapting and learning everyday chores: a SIM card, a room, and a canteen that serves food you can eat. Filipino food is rice-based, often sweet, often pork, and rarely as spicy as Indian food, so students rely on a college mess with Indian cooks, a restaurant running an Indian meal subscription, or their own cooking, which needs basic utensils and permission from the boarding house to use an induction plate in the room. Room sharing is the normal arrangement: two to four students in one room pay ₱10,000 to ₱15,000 a month in Manila and ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 in Cebu and Davao, while a hostel with food, electricity, water and cleaning costs ₱13,000 to ₱15,000. Numbeo's perception index puts the Philippines at 43.33 on crime and 56.67 on safety, against India's 44.16 and 55.84. The Philippines is a friendly country, and people are welcoming and eager to help.

![The CCLEX bridge in Cebu lit red at night, reflecting on the water](https://drdreams.in/about/gallery-cebu-bridge-night.jpg)

*Cebu at night. Small enough to learn in a month, large enough that new places keep turning up.*

## The first month is logistics, not medicine

The arrival month has nothing to do with the course. It is a SIM card, a bank account, a medical check for the visa paperwork, a mattress, a bucket, and working out which canteen will not cause illness. Heat hits first: the air at the airport feels like a wet towel, and a room with a fan that clicks all night is a normal first night.

This fortnight makes many students wonder whether they have made a mistake. That feeling passes faster than it appears to. By the third week there is a routine, a reliable place to eat, and two or three people to message late at night. The whole adjustment rests on one skill: asking strangers for help. Ask the senior student, the landlord and the security guard. They are used to the question.

The first month is not a test of whether you are cut out for medicine. It is a test of whether you can ask for directions, a phone number and a second opinion about a lease.

## Food decides the first year

Filipino food is rice-based, often sweet, often pork, and rarely spicy in the way an Indian student expects. Students who look for dal at every meal end up living on instant noodles. First-year survival frequently comes down to rice and egg. Local staples are good once they are eaten on their own terms: lechon, sinigang, and a breakfast of garlic rice and dried fish.

The practical order is simple. A college mess with Indian cooks is the easiest first year. The next option is a restaurant running an Indian meal subscription. Cooking yourself means basic utensils and written permission from the boarding house, because some do not allow an induction plate inside a room. Manila has enough of an Indian population that spices and restaurants are easy to find. Cebu has Indian restaurants and spice shops in a few areas, but not around every campus. Davao has the least, and Sasa, where Jose Maria sits, has less again.

Where there is no mess, students cook. Learn dal, rice and one vegetable before departure. Carry turmeric, cumin, coriander powder, garam masala and chilli powder in checked luggage, because these are the expensive and hard-to-find part. A rice cooker and an induction plate bought after arrival do the rest. Buying an induction plate is not optional if you plan to cook every day.

Indian food and spices are available around campus in all three cities. The drawback is price: imported groceries cost more than the MRP printed in India because distributors pay import and cargo charges. Budget for that instead of expecting Indian prices.

## Rent and money, month to month

The published 2026 and 2027 college sheets put food and accommodation at 14,000 Philippine pesos a month at Gullas and 15,000 Philippine pesos a month at DMSF, Jose Maria and Brokenshire. Those are college estimates, not a market survey, and they assume shared accommodation and ordinary meals.

Ground reality is room sharing, not one-bedroom listings. Two to four students share one room at ₱10,000 to ₱15,000 a month in Manila and ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 in Cebu and Davao. A hostel costs ₱13,000 to ₱15,000 a month with food, electricity, water and cleaning included. Manila feels slightly more expensive than Cebu and Davao because it is a metropolitan area. The difference is modest, and the gap between cities is smaller than the gap between college fee sheets.

An Indian mess subscription outside college costs ₱2,500 a month for one meal a day, or ₱4,500 to ₱5,000 for two meals a day, depending on the restaurant.

A mobile phone plan with at least ten gigabytes of data costs about ₱861 in Manila, ₱907 in Cebu and ₱715 in Davao in the same Numbeo sample. Beyond rent, the monthly spend is food, transport, phone data and whatever the weekend costs. Cooking cuts that figure more than any other single decision.

Open a local bank account in the first month. Carrying cash for a semester is risky and expensive, and paying tuition through a bank leaves a receipt that matters if anything is ever disputed. Ask the college which bank works with international students, and bring the documents that bank requires.

## Safety, with the numbers

Numbeo's November 2026 perception index puts the Philippines at 43.33 on crime and 56.67 on safety, against India at 44.16 on crime and 55.84 on safety. Those are public perception scores, not police records, and they are not a personal guarantee. The useful point is that the Philippines does not rank as a country students should avoid. Ordinary city sense still applies, and most of it is the same advice given to students in Delhi or Mumbai.

- Do not walk alone at night in an area you do not know yet.
- Do not carry large amounts of cash or wear obvious gold.
- Use Grab rather than unmarked taxis, especially at night and especially in Manila.
- Keep your passport, visa documents and a set of photocopies in different places.
- Learn the local emergency numbers and the college security number in the first week.
- Know the nearest hospital, and do not swim at a beach with a red flag.

The larger risk to a medical career is not crime. It is drifting for two years and then panicking about FMGE. That has cost Indian students more time than anything in the news.

## Getting around, and getting things delivered

Ride-hailing and food delivery work from a phone, the same way Rapido, Swiggy and Zomato work in India. Grab offers four-seater and six-seater GrabCar rides, advance booking for airport trips and upfront pricing, and its GrabFood service delivers meals. Foodpanda is the other main food delivery app. Angkas, MoveIt and Joyride are the motorcycle taxis for short trips; Joyride also carries courier and freight work.

The official sites are [Grab](https://www.grab.com/ph/), [Angkas](https://angkas.com/), [MoveIt](https://moveit.ph/), [Joyride](https://joyride.ph/) and [foodpanda](https://www.foodpanda.ph/).

Jeepneys are the cheapest way to move inside a city. Note the number painted on the jeepney: it marks the route and the stops, so you can work out which one goes your way. For long-distance trips, go to the bus terminal, or book a self-drive car or a car with a driver through Facebook Marketplace, where prices are often the lowest. The same marketplace is active for house listings and second-hand goods.

## Shopping, groceries and local markets

[Shopee](https://shopee.ph/), [Lazada](https://www.lazada.ph/), [Shein](https://ph.shein.com/) and [Temu](https://www.temu.com/ph-en/) are the online shopping sites that work like Flipkart in India. They are usually cheaper than buying in a shop. Delivery takes about four to five days in Metro Manila and seven to eight days in Cebu and Davao. [Facebook Marketplace](https://www.facebook.com/marketplace/) covers cars, rooms, second-hand goods and house listings.

For everyday groceries, the malls and Gaisano stores are cheaper than a convenience shop. Local markets are cheaper again:

- **Cebu:** Carbon Market in downtown Cebu, the largest market in the city and the oldest in Central Visayas, with dry goods, fruit, vegetables and meat. Colon Street nearby is the old shopping street.
- **Manila:** Divisoria in Tondo, Binondo and San Nicolas for low-priced goods, with Tutuban Center and a night market. Quinta Market on Carlos Palanca Street in Quiapo sits beside the Pasig River.
- **Davao:** Bankerohan Public Market, the largest and busiest market in the city, for wet and dry goods.

Map links: [Carbon Market, Cebu](https://www.google.com/maps/search/Carbon+Market+Cebu), [Divisoria, Manila](https://www.google.com/maps/search/Divisoria+Manila), [Quinta Market, Manila](https://www.google.com/maps/search/Quinta+Market+Quiapo+Manila), [Bankerohan Public Market, Davao](https://www.google.com/maps/search/Bankerohan+Public+Market+Davao), and [Gaisano stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaisano_Malls).

## The language

Classes are in English and hospital records are in English. Filipino English follows an American rhythm rather than an Indian one, so the first lecture takes effort. Lecturers switch to Tagalog or Cebuano among themselves. That is normal conversation, not rudeness aimed at foreign students.

Learn a few phrases: salamat for thank you, magkano for how much, and one greeting in the local language. The effort changes how people respond to you more than any amount of grammar.

## Weather, and what it does to a wardrobe

PAGASA, the national weather service, defines two major seasons using temperature and rainfall. The rainy season runs from June to November. The dry season runs from December to May, split into a cool dry season from December to February and a hot dry season from March to May. National annual rainfall ranges from 965 to 4,064 millimeters. General Santos City in Cotabato, near Davao, averages only 978 millimeters a year.

PAGASA also notes that typhoons generally form near the Marianas and Caroline Islands and track north-west, which spares Mindanao from most direct hits. That is the official reason Davao is less exposed than Luzon and the Visayas. It still rains hard there.

Carry light cotton clothes and one sturdy umbrella. Cheap umbrellas break in monsoon wind and need replacing every few weeks; a better one lasts years. Shoes must survive a flooded street. Air conditioning is standard in classrooms and common in hostels, sometimes as a paid extra. A room with air conditioning and a room without are two different rents, and the difference is most obvious in June. Keep documents in a waterproof bag, follow PAGASA rather than a group chat during a storm, and leave a buffer day around any flight in the wet season.

## Homesickness, stated plainly

The first semester is the hardest part of the programme and the brochures do not mention it. Students miss food, family and being understood without effort. Around the third month many are sure they have made a mistake. That week is common, and it ends.

What helps, in order: a routine, three or four people you eat with, one call home at a fixed time each week, and something physical that is not studying. Going home in the first semester does not help, because the adjustment starts again on return. By the second year the city stops feeling temporary for most students. It happens later than anyone wants.

## What to pack

- Light cotton clothes, a few formal outfits for clinical postings, and a white coat if the college does not issue one.
- Basic spices in sealed packets, in checked luggage.
- Prescription medicine in its original packaging, with the prescription.
- A universal adapter and a power bank.
- Paper copies of every document, and digital copies in cloud storage.
- One item that makes the room feel like your own. It matters more than it sounds.

Leave winter clothes and unused gadgets at home. The heat does not let up enough to justify the weight.

## The comparison table

The college matters more than the city. The city decides what an ordinary Tuesday feels like, how much you spend outside tuition, and how easily you can get home. This is the short version. The sections below carry the detail.

Cebu, Manila and Davao for an Indian medical student.

| Factor | Cebu | Manila | Davao |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Colleges covered here | GCM Gullas, Southwestern | Perpetual Help (Las Piñas) | DMSF, Brokenshire, Jose Maria |
| Feel | Calmer second city, walkable pockets, island pace | Dense capital, fast, noisy, always open | Smaller southern city, relaxed, spread out |
| Shared room | ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 | ₱10,000 to ₱15,000 | ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 |
| Indian community | Small but present | Largest | Smallest |
| Traffic | Manageable | The main daily tax | Manageable |
| Typhoon exposure | Exposed | Exposed, with flooding | Less exposed than the other two |
| Flights to India | One stop usually, sometimes direct | Most options, one stop or direct | Usually two stops |

## Cebu

Cebu is the second city of the Philippines: an island, a busy port, an old Spanish core and a great deal of coastline within an hour of the colleges. It is smaller than Manila, cheaper in the city centre and easier to move around. Mactan airport sits on the island, so the trip home starts close.

Two of the six colleges covered here are in Cebu: [GCM Gullas](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#gcm-gullas) in Banilad and [Southwestern University](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#southwestern) in the city. The Indian batch at Gullas is large and the one at Southwestern is smaller. That difference matters more than the postcode.

The trade is that Cebu is not Manila. There are fewer specialists, fewer large public hospital rotations and a smaller Indian community. A student who needs a large diaspora will find Cebu quiet. A student who wants the city to be the calm part of the decision will find it the easiest of the three.

## Manila

Metro Manila is not one city. It is sixteen cities and one municipality, stitched together by highways that are never empty. The college covered here, [University of Perpetual Help](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#perpetual), is in Las Piñas, south of the old city, which is quieter than the centre but still part of the same sprawl.

The advantage is scale. The largest Indian community of the three, the widest choice of Indian restaurants and grocery shops, the largest hospitals and the most flight connections. A student who does not want to be the only Indian in the room will find Manila comfortable.

The cost is time and money. Traffic takes an hour or two a day if you live far from campus. Rent is highest in the city centre. The heat is heavier because the city holds it, and flooding in the wet season is real. Students who manage well live close to campus and treat the wider city as a weekend place.

## Davao

Davao is on Mindanao, in the south. It is cleaner and calmer than Manila, cheaper than both Manila and Cebu, and spread out enough that you will use transport daily. The three colleges here are [DMSF](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#dmsf), [Brokenshire](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#brokenshire) and [Jose Maria](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#jmc).

DMSF has the strongest clinical reputation of the three, with a large patient load and a three-dimensional anatomy laboratory. Brokenshire is smaller, with faculty who know your name and a smaller attached hospital. Jose Maria is the budget option, with medical missions and basic facilities. The spread inside one city is wider than the spread between cities.

The trade is distance. Davao is farther from India than Cebu or Manila, and most routes involve two stops. The Indian community is the smallest of the three and Indian food is harder to find. A student who cooks and wants the lowest total cost will find Davao worth the trade. A student who needs frequent flights home will not.

## Cost of living

Tuition is set by the college. Living cost is set by the city and by whether you cook. The college estimates of 14,000 Philippine pesos a month at Gullas and 15,000 Philippine pesos a month at DMSF, Jose Maria and Brokenshire assume shared accommodation and ordinary meals. Ground figures for a shared room are ₱10,000 to ₱15,000 in Manila and ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 in Cebu and Davao, with hostels at ₱13,000 to ₱15,000 including food and utilities.

Manila costs slightly more than Cebu and Davao because it is a metropolitan area. A shared room there is ₱10,000 to ₱15,000, against ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 in the other two. None of these gaps is as large as the difference between two college fee sheets, so do not pick a city to save rent and then pick a college that costs two lakh more.

The larger variable is food. A student who cooks rice, dal and vegetables most days spends a fraction of what a student spends eating out twice a day. The [cost page](https://drdreams.in/fees-and-cost/index.md) breaks this into lines you can budget.

## Indian food and community

Manila wins on food. Las Piñas and the wider metro have Indian restaurants, spice shops and grocery stores stocking atta, dal, ghee and pickles. Cebu has a smaller but real set of Indian restaurants and spice shops, concentrated in a few areas. Davao has the least, so students cook more and learn to substitute.

Community matters for different reasons. A large Indian batch means company, shared notes and someone to split rent with. It can also become a bubble that keeps you from learning the local language and making Filipino friends. A small batch is lonelier in the first month and usually pushes students into the wider campus. Neither is better. Know which one suits you.

## Safety

All three cities are ordinary places to be a student. The honest differences are about streets and hours. Manila has parts of the metro where you do not walk alone at night, and pickpocketing is a city problem. Cebu is calmer, with the usual advice about unlit streets and late nights. Davao has a reputation for strict local administration and feels orderly, though the usual precautions still apply.

The wider safety issue for Indian students is health, heat and the sea. PAGASA's climate page gives the official weather picture, and the Numbeo index gives the safety comparison. Keep the embassy contact and the college emergency number saved, and do not treat either index as a promise about your own street.

## Hospitals and clinical exposure

Manila has the largest hospitals and the widest case mix. Cebu has strong regional hospitals and a busy port population. Davao has DMSF's hospital network and Brokenshire's smaller attached hospital. For clinical years the question is not the city's hospital count but which hospital your college attaches you to, how many students share each bed and whether foreign students are allowed to examine patients.

Ask that question college by college. A large city with a large hospital is useless if your college sends forty students to one ward and lets them watch. A smaller hospital where students clerk, present and assist is better training. The [college comparison](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md) records hospital exposure for each of the six.

## Weather and typhoons

PAGASA puts the rainy season at June to November and the dry season at December to May, with a cool dry period from December to February and a hot dry period from March to May. Manila floods in heavy rain, especially in low-lying districts. Cebu is exposed to storms crossing the Visayas. Davao is farther south, and PAGASA notes that north-west-tracking typhoons spare Mindanao from most direct hits, although it still gets heavy rain.

Practical advice: keep a rain jacket, waterproof sandals and a power bank. Keep document copies in a waterproof bag. Follow PAGASA rather than a group chat. Do not book a flight home in the middle of a typhoon without a buffer day.

## Flights home

Manila has the most connections to India, usually one stop through Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok or the Gulf, and sometimes direct. Cebu is next, with one stop common and direct routes appearing and disappearing by season. Davao usually means two stops, often through Manila, which adds hours and a connection you can miss.

If you plan to go home every year, price the flights before you choose the city. A cheaper college in Davao can lose its advantage over five years if every trip home costs more and takes a day longer. If you plan to stay through the programme, this matters less.

## Which city suits which student

Pick the city that matches the student, not the brochure.

| If you are... | Start with | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On a tight budget | Davao | Lowest living cost, and Jose Maria is the cheapest college of the six |
| Needing a large Indian community | Manila | Most Indian food, shops and students |
| Wanting a calmer city | Cebu | Smaller, cheaper in the centre, and easier to move around than Manila |
| Planning to fly home every year | Manila or Cebu | Better connections, fewer stops |
| Wanting the strongest clinical volume | Davao (DMSF) | Large patient load and a dedicated anatomy laboratory |
| Wanting small classes | Davao (Brokenshire) | Smaller batches and more faculty attention |

The final decision is still the college, the fee sheet and the NMC requirements. City is the third question, not the first. Read the [college comparison](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md) before you decide on a skyline.

*Check the source*

## Where the figures come from

Prices, weather and safety scores change. These are the sources used on this page, checked on 27 November 2026. Open them before you commit money to a city.

- [Numbeo: crime index, Philippines](https://www.numbeo.com/crime/country_result.jsp?country=Philippines)
- [Numbeo: crime index, India](https://www.numbeo.com/crime/country_result.jsp?country=India)
- [Grab](https://www.grab.com/ph/)
- [Angkas](https://angkas.com/)
- [MoveIt](https://moveit.ph/)
- [Joyride](https://joyride.ph/)
- [foodpanda](https://www.foodpanda.ph/)
- [Shopee](https://shopee.ph/)
- [Lazada](https://www.lazada.ph/)
- [Shein](https://ph.shein.com/)
- [Temu](https://www.temu.com/ph-en/)
- [Facebook Marketplace](https://www.facebook.com/marketplace/)

*Questions*

## What students and parents ask

**Is the Philippines safe for Indian students?**

Numbeo's November 2026 perception index puts the Philippines at 43.33 on crime and 56.67 on safety, against India at 44.16 and 55.84. That is public perception, not police data, and it is not a personal guarantee. Use ordinary city sense: do not walk alone in unfamiliar areas at night, do not flash money, and use ride-hailing rather than unmarked taxis.

**Will I get Indian food?**

In Manila, yes, easily. Cebu has Indian restaurants and spice shops in a few areas. Davao has the least, and students cook more. A college mess with Indian cooks is the easiest first year. Carry turmeric, cumin, coriander powder, garam masala and chilli powder in checked luggage, and buy a rice cooker and an induction plate on arrival.

**What should I pack for the Philippines?**

Light cotton clothes, formal clothes for clinical postings, a white coat if the college does not issue one, basic spices in sealed packets, prescription medicine in its original packaging with the prescription, a universal adapter, a power bank, and copies of every document in both paper and cloud form. Leave winter clothes at home.

**Is Manila better than Cebu for Indian students?**

Neither is better in general. Manila has the largest Indian community, the widest choice of Indian groceries and restaurants, the largest hospitals and the most flight connections. Cebu is calmer, more compact and easier to move around. A room shared by two to four students costs ₱10,000 to ₱15,000 a month in Manila and ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 in Cebu. Choose on the college first, then the city.

**Is Davao safe for Indian students?**

Davao is an ordinary student city with a reputation for strict local administration. PAGASA notes that typhoons moving north-west from the Pacific spare Mindanao from most direct hits, so storm exposure is lower than in Luzon and the Visayas. The usual city precautions still apply: avoid unlit streets at night, keep documents safe, and know the nearest hospital.

**Where is the cheapest place to live?**

Cebu and Davao are the cheapest of the three: a shared room costs ₱8,000 to ₱10,000 a month, against ₱10,000 to ₱15,000 in Manila. A hostel with food and utilities costs ₱13,000 to ₱15,000. The difference between cities is smaller than the difference between college fee sheets.

**Which city has the best hospitals for clinical training?**

Manila has the largest hospitals and the widest case mix, but the hospital your college attaches you to matters more. Ask how many students share each ward and whether foreign students examine patients. A smaller hospital with real patient contact is better training than a large one where students only watch.

**Do I need to speak Tagalog or Cebuano?**

No. Medical teaching and hospital records are in English. Lecturers switch between English, Tagalog and Cebuano among themselves, which is normal and not directed at foreign students. A few phrases help with patients and vendors: salamat for thank you, magkano for how much, and one greeting.

title: "Life Outside Studies in the Philippines: Food, Weekends, Travel"
description: "What the week looks like when you are not studying: food, weekends in Cebu, festivals, sport, travel on a student budget, and how to keep it from eating the degree."
source: https://drdreams.in/life-outside-studies/
updated: 2026-11-25
author: DrDreams
language: en
